blurb: Every repo and skill from the 2 November issue, with what each does and the setup steps from its own README.
intro: Issue #35 had six repos and four AI skills, and this page covers all ten. Most of it is for people building with a coding agent: a plain English map of your app, a game studio template and skills for reviews, design references and module design. Start with Floorplan if you can't say how your app fits together. If you dictate a lot, Hex is the quickest win.

items.name: Floorplan
items.cost: Free (MIT). It runs on your existing Claude or ChatGPT plan, with no API keys.
items.short: Your coding agent reads your codebase and draws an interactive map of it, with every part named in plain English.
items.what: Floorplan is a plugin that maps your app. Scripts scan files, imports, routes and web requests, then the AI names each part and describes each file. You get a zoomable map in `floorplan/index.html` with screens, endpoints, outside services, a Health check and a Recent work view of what your AI just changed.
items.who: People who built an app with AI help and can't say how it fits together, and teams onboarding someone new. It is made for apps you own. To study a big codebase function by function, the README points you to other tools.
needs: Node.js 18 or newer
Claude Code or Codex
Optional: the Claude Code CLI, so the map's Ask bar can read your real code

steps.title: Install in Claude Code
steps.text: Run these in the desktop app's Code tab or the CLI, then start a new session.
steps.code:
claude plugin marketplace add haydenschmitty/floorplan
claude plugin install floorplan@floorplan

steps.title: Or install in Codex
steps.text: In the Codex app you can also open Plugins, choose Add a marketplace, enter `haydenschmitty/floorplan` and install Floorplan.
steps.code:
codex plugin marketplace add haydenschmitty/floorplan
codex plugin add floorplan@floorplan

steps.title: Make your first map
steps.text: Open your project. If your frontend and backend are separate repos, open the folder that holds both. Ask "Make me a floorplan of this app." In Codex you can type `$floorplan`. The map opens with a short tour.

steps.title: Keep it current
steps.text: After more work, ask "Update the floorplan." Only what changed gets re-read, and your latest changes light up under Recent work.

try.label: From the README
try.where: Your coding agent, then the map
try.text: Ask your agent "Fix the important issues from the floorplan's Health check", or ask the map "If I change the users table, what breaks?"

watch: A first map takes a few minutes for a small app and longer for a big one. It uses your Claude or ChatGPT plan like any other task.
The AI reads your files through your own account. The map and its local server stay on your machine and only accept local connections.
It writes a `floorplan/` folder, and in Claude Code, if you say yes, a section in `CLAUDE.local.md`. Neither is committed.
The README says the Health check catches the classic mistakes in AI-built apps and is no substitute for a full audit.

items.name: OpenDuet
items.cost: Free (MIT). You pay for your own model key. It needs a CopilotKit Intelligence project, and the free Developer plan is enough.
items.works_with: Self-hosted web app, Slack, Microsoft Teams; OpenAI or Anthropic models
items.short: A self-hosted agent that reads your mail and calendar, sends a morning brief and asks before it sends, pays, signs or deletes.
items.what: OpenDuet is a proactive assistant built on CopilotKit's OpenBot platform. Each agent gets its own container with a browser, a `/workspace` folder and a shell, so it keeps working while you're away. It reads Gmail and Google Calendar, sorts what needs you from what can wait, and routes every action through a gateway that checks your policy and logs it.
items.who: Developers who want to run and customise their own assistant and are fine with Docker, env files and Google OAuth setup. It is early and in active development, so skip it if you want a finished hosted product. There is no hosted or deploy guide yet.
needs: Docker
Bun 1.3 or newer
Node, for `npx`
A model key (OpenAI by default, or Anthropic)
A CopilotKit Intelligence project
Optional: a Google OAuth client for Gmail and Calendar

steps.title: Clone and install
steps.text: Run every command from the repository root.
steps.code:
git clone https://github.com/CopilotKit/OpenDuet.git
cd OpenDuet
cp .env.example .env
bun install

steps.title: Pick an Intelligence project
steps.text: The last command copies the key to `INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY`, which the server reads, and sets up the Learning container.
steps.code:
npx --yes copilotkit@latest login
npx --yes copilotkit@latest project select
bun openbot/scripts/setup-learning.ts

steps.title: Add your model key
steps.text: Put it in `.env`. For Anthropic instead, set `BOT_PROVIDER=anthropic` and `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.

steps.title: Start it
steps.text: This starts Postgres and each Bot's computer in Docker, runs migrations and starts the app. Open http://localhost:3010. `bash scripts/stop.sh` stops it.

steps.title: Optional: try Google with the fake
steps.text: A fake Google with an invented inbox ships for tests. Set `OPENDUET_FAKE_GOOGLE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:4900` in `.env`, restart, then follow the README's steps to enable and connect it.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Ask the OpenDuet Bot to do something in its own browser and watch it work on its computer. Then choose what it must ask you about first in `/settings/approvals`.

watch: The CopilotKit runtime sends usage telemetry to CopilotKit. Set `COPILOTKIT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=true` or `DO_NOT_TRACK=1` to turn it off.
Once connected it reads your Gmail and calendar. It sends a reply only after you answer.
Each agent has its own browser and shell. Its defaults ask before anything that sends, pays, signs or deletes, and a message to other people always asks first.
Web research tools share data with outside providers. The README says an administrator should review those risks before granting them.
It is early software and things will move. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

items.name: The Day Trader skill
items.cost: Free (MIT). No signup and no API key for the data tools.
items.works_with: Claude Code, or any chat as a plain SKILL.md
items.short: 11 AI skills for day trading that scan charts, track news, plan entries and exits, and simulate a trade before you risk money.
items.what: A pack of 11 skills backed by plain Python tools that read free public data from Yahoo Finance, Nasdaq Trader, SEC EDGAR and the House Clerk. They run in a chain: scan for setups, check news, time the entry, plan the exit, replay the trade 10,000 times, size it, check your limits and only then build an order. Everything lands in a `trader/` folder.
items.who: People who already day trade and want a disciplined checklist with real numbers. The README says most people who day trade lose money and that this is not financial advice. Skip it if you're new to trading.
needs: Claude Code, or any chat that accepts a pasted SKILL.md
Python 3.8 or newer (nothing to pip install)
Your name and email for the SEC tools
Optional: a brokerage connector such as Alpaca's MCP server, for orders

steps.title: Install as a plugin
steps.text: Plugin skills show up namespaced, like `/day-trader-skill:trader-scanner`.

steps.title: Or copy the folders
steps.text: This gives plain names like `/trader-scanner`. Copy into your repo's `.claude/skills/` instead to keep it to one project.

steps.title: Identify yourself to the SEC
steps.text: Put this in `trader/config.json`, or set the `SEC_USER_AGENT` environment variable.

steps.title: Run a scan
steps.text: Start with `/trader-scanner`, then follow the chain: news, entry, exit, timemachine, budget, risk, broker.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Look for opening range breakouts so far today with `python3 trader-scanner/scan.py orb --at 10:15`, then replay a planned trade with `python3 trader-timemachine/timemachine.py run --write`.

watch: Not financial advice. The README says you can lose money.
Only `/trader-broker` can lead to an order, and only after `/trader-risk` passes it and you type yes. Set your brokerage tool to Needs approval, never Always allow.
Paper trading is the default. Keys live in environment variables, never in the chat.
Yahoo Finance's chart endpoint is not an official API. It can lag, change or rate-limit you, so check against your broker.
The Time Machine is a simulation from the last 60 days of bars, not a prediction.

items.name: Claude Code Game Studios
items.works_with: Claude Code; Godot 4, Unity, Unreal Engine 5
items.short: A project template that runs a Claude Code session like a game studio, with 49 agents, 74 skills and 15 hooks.
items.what: You clone it as the starting point for your game. It gives your session directors, department leads and specialists, each with set duties and review gates, plus slash commands for every phase from brainstorm to release. A `modes.rigor` setting decides how much process it enforces, and the default `minimal` is the lightest.
items.who: Solo developers and small teams making a game with Claude Code who want structure and review. The agents ask before they write, so it isn't autopilot. If you want a game generated for you in one go, this isn't that.
needs: Git
Claude Code
Python 3, which every skill and hook uses to read `project.yaml`
Bash (comes with Git for Windows on Windows)
Recommended: jq

steps.title: Start Claude Code in the root folder
steps.text: Use the folder that holds `CLAUDE.md` and `project.yaml`. Starting in a subfolder skips the hooks, deny rules and ask-first mode.

steps.title: Run /start
steps.text: It asks where you are, from no idea to existing work, and sends you to the right workflow. It also writes `project.yaml` for you.

steps.title: Or jump straight in
steps.text: Use `/brainstorm` for ideas, `/setup-engine godot 4.7` to set your engine, or `/project-stage-detect` on an existing project.

steps.title: Change the process weight
steps.text: View settings with `/settings`, or raise rigor when the project grows.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Run `/start`, pick vague concept, and let `/brainstorm` write a one-page brief. Then go `/create-stories` and `/dev-story`.

watch: 15 hooks run on every session. Most exit at once when the command or file isn't relevant. A commit that stages data JSON is blocked if Python is missing.
Permission rules in `settings.json` auto-allow test runs and block force push, `rm -rf` and reading `.env` files.
The three director agents ask for Opus and 16 others name Sonnet. The rest use your session's model.
The README measured that the heavier `standard` rigor wrote 30 docs before any code and did not make a better game.

items.name: Hex
items.short: Local voice dictation. Hold a key, speak, and it types what you said into whatever app you're in.
items.what: Hex transcribes speech on your device and pastes the text into the app you're using. You hold a shortcut, speak and let go. Experimental features sit in Labs, at the bottom of the sidebar.
items.who: Anyone who wants dictation that doesn't send audio to a server once it's set up. The macOS download is for Apple silicon only.
needs: A Mac with Apple silicon, a Windows x64 or ARM64 PC, or Linux on x86_64 or ARM64
A microphone

steps.title: Download it
steps.text: The README has stable and dev builds for each platform: a DMG for Mac, installers for Windows, and an executable, .deb or .rpm for Linux. Stable is the current release: https://github.com/anomalyco/hex

steps.title: Or on Linux
steps.text: Use the AUR, Nix or the install script. The script pipes a download into your shell.
steps.code:
yay -S hex-bin
nix profile add github:anomalyco/hex
curl -fsSL https://anoma.ly/hex/install-linux.sh | sh

steps.title: Dictate
steps.text: Hold the shortcut, speak, then let go. Hex pastes into the app you're in.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Click into a text box, hold the shortcut, say a sentence and let go.

watch: The first run downloads a speech model. After that, the README says nothing leaves your machine.
The Linux install script pipes a download straight into your shell. Read the script first, or use a package.
Dev builds update themselves from the dev channel.
The project doesn't take pull requests. Open an issue instead.

items.name: OmniDiff
items.cost: Free (AGPL-3.0). A paid commercial licence is available through GitHub Sponsors.
items.works_with: Linux, macOS, Windows; git, jj, VS Code, Neovim
items.short: A content-aware diff tool in Rust that shows what really changed in code, pictures, fonts, archives and PDFs.
items.what: OmniDiff diffs 25 languages structurally with tree-sitter, so it highlights the part of a line that changed. It also diffs pictures pixel by pixel, fonts glyph by glyph, archives file by file and PDFs page by page. It has a terminal viewer, a plain text mode for scripts, JSON output and setup wizards for git and jj.
items.who: Developers who review a lot of diffs, especially with binary assets that git just calls different. If your company can't use AGPL software, you'd need the commercial licence.
needs: One of: Homebrew, apt, Nix, a prebuilt binary, or a Rust toolchain (rustc 1.92 or later) with a C compiler
git or jj, for version control use

steps.title: Install with Homebrew
steps.text: On macOS and Linux. Prebuilt binaries are also on the GitHub releases page.

steps.title: Or build from source
steps.text: The first build takes a few minutes.

steps.title: Or on Debian and Ubuntu
steps.text: This adds a signed apt repository.
steps.code:
sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/apt/keyrings
curl -fsSL https://ivankovic.github.io/omnidiff/apt/omnidiff-archive-keyring.gpg \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/keyrings/omnidiff-archive-keyring.gpg > /dev/null
echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/omnidiff-archive-keyring.gpg] \
https://ivankovic.github.io/omnidiff/apt stable main" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/omnidiff.list > /dev/null
sudo apt update && sudo apt install omnidiff

steps.title: Compare two files
steps.text: Press `?` in the viewer for the keys.

steps.title: Hook it into git
steps.text: The wizard asks whether to set it up globally or for this repo. Then use `git difftool` for the full viewer. For jj, run `omnidiff jj configure`.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Run `GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF=omnidiff git diff` in a repo with a changed image or font and see what changed inside it.

watch: It is AGPL-3.0. Organisations that can't meet AGPL terms need the paid commercial licence.
`git diff` and `git log -p` always get plain text. Only `git difftool` opens the interactive viewer.
PDF support has fewer than ten judged test cases, and only 57% of PDFs diff in under 100ms.

items.name: review-document
items.short: Turns review findings you already have into one short Markdown write-up: verdict first, each finding ranked with evidence and a fix.
items.what: The skill organises a code, design or QA review into a document the reader can act on. It starts with a verdict (approve, approve with changes, request changes or blocked), ranks findings as blocking, should fix or nit, and gives each one a location, evidence and the smallest fix. It ends with what you checked and what you didn't, then lints the page with the Comark linter.
items.who: People who write reviews or audits for someone else to act on. It doesn't find problems for you. It only writes up findings you already have.
needs: A coding agent that supports skills
Vite+ (`vp`) or pnpm, for the install and the lint step

steps.title: Add the skills
steps.text: This is the README's install command for the repo's agent skills. It names the `comark-ui` skill, so check that review-document is in the list it offers. Without Vite+, `pnpm dlx` takes the same arguments.

steps.title: Give it your findings
steps.text: Ask your agent to write up the review. It picks a verdict, merges findings with one cause and ranks them blocking first.

steps.title: Lint the result
steps.text: The skill runs this and fixes problems until there are none. Then read the rendered page once as the reader would.
steps.code: vp dlx --package comark-linter --package comark-ui comark-lint review.md

try.label: A first prompt
try.text: "Write up the findings from this code review as a review document."

watch: It organises findings. The review itself is still your job.
The output uses Comark blocks such as `::diff` and `::tests`, so it renders best where Comark UI is set up.
The README's only skill install command names the `comark-ui` skill, not review-document.

items.name: gather
items.works_with: Coding agents that support skills, Claude Code plugin
items.short: Collects design references from your own saves, boards and pattern sites onto one linked board before you start a design.
items.what: Before a design is built, gather turns your brief into short searches and runs them across every connected source at once, such as Pond, marked.dev, Are.na, Cosmos, Pinterest and Mobbin. A bundled collector downloads the images and fills one local board as results land. Each reference gets a note on the part to take and a link back to its source.
items.who: Designers and front-end developers who want inspiration for one screen or part, gathered in one place. It does the most when you've connected your own libraries and boards.
needs: A coding agent that supports skills
Node, to run the bundled collector
Accounts on the reference sources you want to search

steps.title: Install the collection
steps.text: This adds all the skills in the repo, gather included.

steps.title: Or as a Claude Code plugin
steps.text: Plugin skills take a prefix, such as `/userinterface:audit`.

steps.title: Ask for inspiration
steps.text: gather applies on its own when you ask for references or inspo. Name the screen, the platform and what you want to look at. It asks once about sources you haven't connected.

steps.title: Review the board
steps.text: The collector serves the board locally and fills it live. Copy your picks back to the agent as the brief for the next step.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Ask for references for a desktop settings page, looking for grouping and density. With no number given, it gathers at least 20 from three sources or more.

watch: It downloads every image and video into a `.gather/` folder, which stays out of version control.
When Mobbin warns that monthly usage is high, it stops searching Mobbin.
When a source needs a login or a CAPTCHA, it stops and asks you.

items.name: ux
items.works_with: Coding agents working in the LobeHub codebase
items.short: LobeHub's own UX checklists for empty, loading and error states, lists at scale, drafts and buttons, for building its screens.
items.what: This is the skill LobeHub uses when building or reviewing user-facing flows in its own app. It covers four design values, a few interaction principles and checklists grouped by what the user is doing: reading, editing, acting, waiting on feedback and discovering features. It points to LobeHub components such as `NavItem` and its `DESIGN.md`.
items.who: People contributing to LobeHub. Anyone else can read the checklists for ideas, but much of it refers to LobeHub's own components and files.
needs: Git and pnpm, to clone LobeHub for local development
A coding agent that reads skills

steps.title: Clone LobeHub
steps.text: These are the README's local development steps. The skill lives in the repo at `.agents/skills/ux`.
steps.code:
git clone https://github.com/lobehub/lobehub.git
cd lobehub
pnpm install

steps.title: Work on a screen
steps.text: The skill isn't called by name. It applies when your agent designs or builds a user-facing flow. Start with its quick review checklist, then read the module for the surface you're on.

try.label: A first prompt
try.where: Your coding agent, in the LobeHub repo
try.text: "Review this list page against the ux skill's Read checklist."

watch: The README gives no install command for the skill on its own. It comes with the LobeHub repo.
It assumes LobeHub's components and `DESIGN.md`, so outside that codebase parts of it won't apply.

items.name: codebase-design
items.works_with: Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, Cursor and other agents
items.short: Gives your agent a shared vocabulary for deep modules, so it designs interfaces that are small, testable and easy to navigate.
items.what: The skill teaches the agent to design deep modules: a lot of behaviour behind a small interface, placed at a clean seam and tested through that interface. It defines terms like module, interface, seam, adapter, depth, leverage and locality, and asks the agent to use them exactly. It also includes the deletion test and rules for testable code.
items.who: Developers whose AI-built codebase is getting hard to change. Other skills in the pack, such as `/improve-codebase-architecture`, lean on it. It's model-invoked, so the agent reaches for it when the task fits.
needs: A supported coding agent

steps.title: Install in Claude Code
steps.text: The plugin updates itself.

steps.title: Or in Codex
steps.code:
codex plugin marketplace add mattpocock/skills
codex plugin add mattpocock-skills@mattpocock

steps.title: Or any other agent
steps.text: Include `setup-matt-pocock-skills` when it asks which skills to take. Pick one install method per agent, or you get every skill twice.
steps.code: npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills -a <agent>  # cursor, opencode, devin, windsurf, amp, pi; omit -a to choose

steps.title: Set up each repo
steps.text: Run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` once per repo. It asks about your issue tracker, triage labels and where to save docs.

steps.title: Ask about a module
steps.text: Ask your agent to design or improve a module's interface. It applies the skill when the task fits.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Run `/improve-codebase-architecture` to scan for deepening opportunities, then pick one to work through.

watch: Skills installed with `npx skills` don't update themselves. Run `npx skills@latest update`.
The README says `/improve-codebase-architecture` is a survey that finds candidates. It won't untangle an old codebase for you.
